questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of connective tissue?

options.text: Cells are tightly packed with little extracellular matrix
options.explanation: That describes epithelial tissue. Connective tissue has abundant ECM with scattered cells.

options.text: Abundant extracellular matrix with scattered cells
options.explanation: Connective tissue is defined by an abundant extracellular matrix (fibers and ground substance) with cells dispersed within it.
Layered arrangement is typical of epithelia, not connective tissue.
Many connective tissues (e.g., bone, areolar) are highly vascular; cartilage is avascular but not all.
Connective tissue mainly arises from mesoderm (mesenchyme).

explanation.overview: Connective tissue is characterized by abundant extracellular matrix, consisting of protein fibers and ground substance, with cells dispersed throughout. It provides support, binds tissues, and mediates nutrient exchange.
explanation.highYield: Connective tissue = few cells + lots of ECM (fibers + ground substance).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Excessive ECM deposition leads to fibrosis in organs like liver and lung.

questions.question: The primary cell type responsible for producing collagen fibers in connective tissue is the:

options.explanation: Macrophages are phagocytic immune cells, not ECM producers.
Mast cells release histamine and heparin, not collagen.
Fibroblasts synthesize and secrete collagen, elastin, and ground substance components.
Adipocytes store fat, not major collagen producers.
Plasma cells produce antibodies.

explanation.overview: Fibroblasts are the most common cells in connective tissue proper, responsible for synthesizing collagen, elastic fibers, and the ground substance.
explanation.highYield: Fibroblast = factory of connective tissue ECM (collagen, GAGs).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Activated fibroblasts (myofibroblasts) contribute to wound contraction and fibrosis.

questions.question: Which type of collagen forms the characteristic banded fibrils seen in electron microscopy?

options.explanation: Type I collagen is the most abundant and forms thick fibrils with 67 nm banding pattern.
Type II collagen is found in cartilage, also has banding but Type I is classic for banded fibrils.
Type III (reticular) fibers are thin and do not form thick banded fibrils.
Type IV forms a meshwork in basement membranes, not fibrils.
Type VII forms anchoring fibrils, not typical banded fibrils.

explanation.overview: Type I collagen assembles into thick fibrils with a repeating 67 nm D-periodic banding pattern, visible by electron microscopy. It is abundant in skin, bone, tendons, and ligaments.
explanation.highYield: Type I collagen = thick fibrils, 67 nm banding; most abundant collagen.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone) is due to defective Type I collagen.

questions.question: Reticular fibers are composed primarily of which collagen type?

options.explanation: Type I forms thick fibrils, not reticular networks.
Type II is in cartilage.
Reticular fibers (type III collagen) form delicate networks supporting soft tissues like lymph nodes and spleen.
Type IV is in basement membrane.
Type V is a minor fibrillar collagen, often co-assembles with type I.

explanation.overview: Reticular fibers consist of type III collagen arranged in a delicate meshwork. They are PAS-positive due to high carbohydrate content and provide a supporting framework in hematopoietic and lymphoid organs.
explanation.highYield: Reticular fibers = Type III collagen; found in lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Silver impregnation stains reticular fibers black, useful for evaluating liver fibrosis.

questions.question: Elastic fibers are composed of:

options.explanation: Collagen is not a major component of elastic fibers.
Elastic fibers contain a core of elastin surrounded by microfibrils of fibrillin.
Reticulin is Type III collagen, not elastic.
Fibrillin forms the microfibrillar scaffold, but mature elastic fibers also contain elastin.
Elastin is the core, but fibrillin microfibrils are essential.

explanation.overview: Elastic fibers provide stretch and recoil. They have an amorphous elastin core surrounded by a sheath of fibrillin microfibrils.
explanation.highYield: Elastic fiber = elastin (core) + fibrillin (microfibrils); stretchable.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Marfan syndrome results from fibrillin-1 mutations, leading to aortic aneurysms.

questions.question: The ground substance of connective tissue is rich in:

options.explanation: Collagen fibers are part of the ECM but ground substance refers to the amorphous gel.
Ground substance consists of GAGs (e.g., hyaluronic acid) and proteoglycans, providing hydration and resistance to compression.
Elastic fibers are fibrous, not ground substance.
Reticular fibers are fibrous.
Ground substance contains GAGs, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins, but GAGs are the main component.

explanation.overview: Ground substance is the amorphous, gel-like material filling spaces between cells and fibers. It contains glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), proteoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins, enabling diffusion of nutrients.
explanation.highYield: Ground substance = GAGs (hyaluronic acid) + proteoglycans; hydration and diffusion.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Degradation of ground substance by hyaluronidase (bacterial) facilitates tissue invasion.

questions.question: Which GAG does NOT contain sulfate and is not covalently linked to a protein core?

options.explanation: Chondroitin sulfate is sulfated and linked to core protein.
Keratan sulfate is sulfated and linked to core protein.
Dermatan sulfate is sulfated and attached to core protein.
Heparan sulfate is sulfated and linked to core protein.
Hyaluronic acid is a non‑sulfated GAG that exists free in the ECM, attracting water and resisting compression.

explanation.overview: Hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan) is unique among GAGs: it is extremely long, unsulfated, and not linked to a protein core. It is synthesized at the cell surface and forms large complexes that create a hydrated gel.
explanation.highYield: Hyaluronic acid = unsulfated, no protein core; excellent lubricant and shock absorber.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hyaluronic acid injections are used for osteoarthritis to restore joint lubrication.

questions.question: Loose (areolar) connective tissue is characterized by:

options.explanation: That describes dense connective tissue.
Areolar tissue has many cells and loosely arranged fibers.

options.text: Randomly arranged fibers with abundant ground substance
options.explanation: Areolar tissue has loosely arranged fibers with ample ground substance and a variety of cell types.
That describes dense regular connective tissue.
That describes elastic tissue.

explanation.overview: Areolar connective tissue is a loose, flexible tissue with a mix of collagen and elastic fibers and abundant ground substance. It supports epithelium and surrounds small blood vessels.
explanation.highYield: Areolar = loose, mixed fibers, high ground substance; many cell types.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Areolar tissue provides a plane for fluid movement during inflammation (edema).

questions.question: Dense irregular connective tissue is found in:

options.explanation: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue.
Ligaments are mostly dense regular, some elastic.
The dermis contains dense irregular connective tissue, with collagen fibers arranged in multiple directions to resist tension.
Aorta has elastic tissue, not dense irregular.
Cornea has highly organized regular lamellae.

explanation.overview: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen bundles oriented in various directions, providing strength against multidirectional forces. It forms the dermis, organ capsules, and submucosa.
explanation.highYield: Dense irregular = dermis, organ capsules; collagen in multiple directions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Scars involve dense irregular connective tissue with less organized collagen.

questions.question: Dense regular connective tissue, with parallel collagen bundles, is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Skin dermis is dense irregular.
Tendons and ligaments have dense regular connective tissue aligned along lines of stress.
Arteries have a mix of smooth muscle and elastic fibers.
Lung is mostly elastic and loose connective.
Bone is specialized connective tissue with mineralized matrix.

explanation.overview: Dense regular connective tissue has tightly packed, parallel collagen fibers and few cells (fibrocytes). It is adapted to resist unidirectional tensile forces.
explanation.highYield: Tendons/ligaments = dense regular CT; parallel collagen bundles.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tendon injuries heal slowly due to poor blood supply.

questions.question: Elastic connective tissue is abundant in the:

options.explanation: Achilles tendon is dense regular, not predominantly elastic.
Elastic tissue (e.g., ligamentum nuchae, aorta) contains many elastic fibers to provide elasticity.
Dermis is dense irregular, contains some elastic but not predominantly.
Cornea has regular collagenous lamellae.
Cartilage is a different connective tissue type.

explanation.overview: Elastic connective tissue, composed of abundant elastic fibers, is found in structures that require stretching and recoil, such as the ligamentum nuchae, ligamentum flavum, and large elastic arteries.
explanation.highYield: Elastic CT = elastic fibers predominate; aorta, ligamentum nuchae.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Aging leads to loss of elastic fibers, contributing to arteriosclerosis.

questions.question: Mucous connective tissue (Wharton's jelly) is found in the:

options.explanation: Adult dermis is dense irregular, not mucous.
Wharton's jelly is a gelatinous mucous connective tissue in the umbilical cord.
Tendons are dense regular.
Bone marrow is hematopoietic tissue.
Lymph nodes contain reticular connective tissue.

explanation.overview: Mucous connective tissue (Wharton's jelly) is a primitive, gelatinous tissue with abundant hyaluronic acid and few collagen fibers. It is present in the umbilical cord, protecting blood vessels.
explanation.highYield: Wharton's jelly = mucous CT; umbilical cord; high hyaluronic acid, few cells.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Wharton's jelly is a source of mesenchymal stem cells.

questions.question: Mesenchyme is embryonic connective tissue that gives rise to:

options.explanation: Mesenchyme gives rise to many tissues, not only bone.

options.text: All connective tissues, muscle, and blood vessels
options.explanation: Mesenchyme differentiates into all types of connective tissue, smooth muscle, and blood vessels.
More than cartilage.
It forms dense, bone, cartilage, etc.
Blood cells arise from hematopoietic stem cells, not mesenchyme directly.

explanation.overview: Mesenchyme is the pluripotent embryonic connective tissue derived mainly from mesoderm. It contains stellate mesenchymal cells and amorphous ground substance, giving rise to all adult connective tissues, as well as muscle and vascular components.
explanation.highYield: Mesenchyme = embryonic stem tissue → all connective tissues, smooth muscle, vessels.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from bone marrow are used in regenerative medicine.

questions.question: Macrophages are derived from:

options.explanation: Fibroblasts are mesenchymal in origin, not hematopoietic.
Macrophages originate from blood monocytes and are part of the mononuclear phagocyte system.
Lymphocytes are a separate lineage.
Mast cells arise from bone marrow precursors.
Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes.

explanation.overview: Macrophages are tissue-resident phagocytes that differentiate from circulating monocytes. They are key effectors of innate immunity and tissue repair.
explanation.highYield: Macrophage = differentiated monocyte; phagocytosis, antigen presentation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Kupffer cells (liver), microglia (CNS), and osteoclasts are specialized macrophages.

questions.question: The function of mast cells includes:

options.explanation: Mast cells are not phagocytes.
Antibodies are produced by plasma cells.

options.text: Release of histamine and heparin in allergic reactions
options.explanation: Mast cells release histamine, heparin, and other mediators in response to allergens.
Collagen synthesis is a fibroblast function.
Lipid storage is in adipocytes.

explanation.overview: Mast cells are granulated cells containing histamine, heparin, and serine proteases. They are activated by IgE cross-linking in type I hypersensitivity reactions.
explanation.highYield: Mast cells = histamine + heparin; IgE receptors; anaphylaxis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn sodium) are used for allergic conditions.

questions.question: Plasma cells are derived from B lymphocytes and function to:

options.explanation: Phagocytosis is macrophage function.
Plasma cells are antibody‑producing cells with a characteristic clock‑face nucleus.
Histamine is from mast cells.
Lipid storage is adipocyte.
Collagen is from fibroblasts.

explanation.overview: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes that produce large amounts of a single antibody specificity. They have a round, eccentrically placed nucleus with clumped chromatin (cartwheel/clock-face).
explanation.highYield: Plasma cell = antibody factory; clock-face nucleus, abundant rough ER.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells.

questions.question: Adipocytes in white adipose tissue contain:

options.explanation: White adipocytes are unilocular, storing energy as one large fat droplet.
That describes brown adipocytes.
Adipocytes store fat, not glycogen.
Brown adipocytes have abundant mitochondria, white adipocytes have few.
Adipocytes are defined by lipid storage.

explanation.overview: White adipose tissue consists of unilocular adipocytes that contain a single, large lipid droplet, pushing the nucleus to the periphery. It stores energy, insulates, and secretes adipokines.
explanation.highYield: White fat = one big lipid droplet; energy storage, insulation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Excess white adipose tissue (obesity) is a risk factor for metabolic syndrome.

questions.question: Brown adipose tissue is characterized by:

options.explanation: Unilocular is white fat.

options.text: Multilocular lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria
options.explanation: Brown adipocytes are multilocular with many mitochondria, enabling non‑shivering thermogenesis.
Brown fat has abundant mitochondria.
It's adipose tissue, not fibrous.
Brown fat is highly vascularized.

explanation.overview: Brown adipose tissue contains multilocular adipocytes with multiple small lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria expressing uncoupling protein-1 (UCP1), which generates heat instead of ATP.
explanation.highYield: Brown fat = many small fat droplets + lots of mitochondria; thermogenesis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Brown fat is prominent in newborns; its activation is a target for obesity treatment.

questions.question: Which cell type is responsible for storing and metabolizing vitamin A?

options.explanation: Hepatic stellate cells in the liver store vitamin A and produce extracellular matrix.
Kupffer cells are liver macrophages.
Fibroblasts do not store large amounts of vitamin A.
Adipocytes store fat, not specifically vitamin A.
Not a primary vitamin A store.

explanation.overview: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) reside in the perisinusoidal space of Disse. They store vitamin A in lipid droplets and are the main producers of ECM in liver fibrosis.
explanation.highYield: Ito cells = vitamin A storage, ECM production; activated in cirrhosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Activated stellate cells are the primary source of excessive collagen in liver cirrhosis.

questions.question: Osteoblasts are derived from:

options.explanation: Osteoclasts are from monocyte lineage.
Osteocytes are mature osteoblasts, not precursors.
Osteoprogenitor cells differentiate into osteoblasts, which form bone.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells.
Fibroblasts are not bone cell precursors.

explanation.overview: Osteoprogenitor cells are mesenchymal stem cells located in the periosteum and endosteum. They proliferate and differentiate into bone-forming osteoblasts.
explanation.highYield: Osteoblast lineage: osteoprogenitor → osteoblast → osteocyte.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bone formation markers include alkaline phosphatase and osteocalcin.

questions.question: Osteoclasts are derived from:

options.explanation: Osteoblasts are different lineage.
Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells formed by fusion of hematopoietic precursors (monocyte lineage).
Osteocytes are former osteoblasts.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells.
Fibroblasts are connective tissue cells.

explanation.overview: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells that resorb bone. They originate from the fusion of monocyte/macrophage precursors under the influence of RANKL and M-CSF.
explanation.highYield: Osteoclast = hematopoietic origin (monocyte fusion); bone resorption.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bisphosphonates and denosumab inhibit osteoclast activity to treat osteoporosis.

questions.question: The periosteum contains which type of connective tissue?

options.explanation: The outer fibrous layer of periosteum is dense irregular connective tissue.
That's tendons/ligaments.
Inner layer is more cellular, but outer is dense irregular.
Not primarily elastic.
Mucous tissue is embryonic.

explanation.overview: The periosteum has two layers: an outer fibrous layer of dense irregular connective tissue and an inner cambium (cellular) layer containing osteoprogenitor cells.
explanation.highYield: Periosteum outer = dense irregular CT; inner = osteoprogenitor cells.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Periosteal elevation is used in surgical approaches to bone.

questions.question: The extracellular matrix of cartilage is rich in:

options.text: Type I collagen and hyaluronic acid
options.explanation: Type I is in bone, not hyaline cartilage.
Hyaline cartilage matrix contains type II collagen and aggrecan (proteoglycan).
Type III is reticular; elastin is in elastic cartilage.
That's basement membrane.
That's elastic fibers, not cartilage matrix.

explanation.overview: Cartilage matrix is composed of type II collagen fibrils and large proteoglycan aggregates (aggrecan) that entangle with hyaluronic acid, providing resilience and compressive strength.
explanation.highYield: Cartilage = type II collagen + aggrecan; GAGs attract water.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteoarthritis involves degradation of aggrecan and type II collagen.

questions.question: Chondrocytes are found in spaces called:

options.explanation: Chondrocytes reside in lacunae within the cartilage matrix.
Canaliculi are in bone, not cartilage.
Haversian canals are in bone.
Volkmann's canals are in bone.
Lamellae are bone layers.

explanation.overview: Cartilage lacunae are cavities in the matrix that house chondrocytes. Unlike bone lacunae, they lack canaliculi; nutrients diffuse through the matrix.
explanation.highYield: Chondrocytes in lacunae; no canaliculi in cartilage.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Chondrocyte apoptosis leads to empty lacunae, seen in osteoarthritis.

questions.question: Which type of cartilage contains abundant elastic fibers?

options.explanation: Hyaline has fine collagen II, not abundant elastic.
Fibrocartilage has type I collagen bundles.
Elastic cartilage (e.g., ear, epiglottis) has elastic fibers for flexibility.
Calcified cartilage is mineralized.
Articular cartilage is hyaline.

explanation.overview: Elastic cartilage contains a dense network of elastic fibers in addition to type II collagen. It is flexible and found in the external ear, epiglottis, and laryngeal cartilages.
explanation.highYield: Elastic cartilage = type II collagen + elastic fibers; ear, epiglottis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cauliflower ear deformity results from trauma to auricular elastic cartilage.

questions.question: Fibrocartilage is characterized by:

options.text: Dense regular collagen bundles with rows of chondrocytes
options.explanation: Fibrocartilage (e.g., intervertebral discs) has thick collagen bundles and rows of chondrocytes.
That describes elastic cartilage.
Hyaline cartilage has higher proteoglycan.
Fibrocartilage is rich in collagen.
Its matrix is fibrocartilaginous, not hyaline.

explanation.overview: Fibrocartilage is a transitional tissue with features of dense regular connective tissue and cartilage. It contains parallel bundles of type I collagen with rows of chondrocytes, providing tensile strength and resistance to compression.
explanation.highYield: Fibrocartilage = type I collagen + chondrocyte rows; intervertebral discs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Degeneration of fibrocartilage in discs can lead to herniation.

questions.question: Osteocytes are connected to each other via:

options.explanation: Osteocyte processes extend through canaliculi and communicate via gap junctions.
Tight junctions are in epithelia, not bone.
Desmosomes are for cell-cell adhesion, not primary in osteocyte communication.
Synapses are neuronal.
Hemidesmosomes attach cells to basement membrane.

explanation.overview: Osteocytes reside in lacunae and extend dendritic processes through canaliculi. These processes are connected by gap junctions, allowing exchange of nutrients, waste, and signals.
explanation.highYield: Osteocyte network = canaliculi + gap junctions; mechanosensation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of osteocyte connectivity contributes to bone fragility.

questions.question: The basic structural unit of compact bone is the:

options.explanation: Trabecula is the unit of spongy bone.
Osteons are cylindrical units with concentric lamellae around a central canal.
Lamellae are layers within an osteon.
Canaliculi are minute channels.
Lacunae are spaces for osteocytes.

explanation.overview: The osteon (Haversian system) consists of concentric rings of bone matrix (lamellae) surrounding a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels. It is the functional unit of compact bone.
explanation.highYield: Osteon = concentric lamellae + central canal; structural unit of compact bone.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteonal remodeling is targeted therapy for microdamage repair.

questions.question: Interstitial lamellae in bone are:

options.explanation: Interstitial lamellae fill the spaces between intact osteons, representing old osteon fragments.
New bone is deposited as concentric lamellae.
Circumferential lamellae are at the outer/inner surface.
That is marrow space.
Periosteal bone is outer circumferential.

explanation.overview: Interstitial lamellae are the irregular, angular fragments of old osteons that remain after bone remodeling. They lie between intact osteons and are evidence of previous remodeling cycles.
explanation.highYield: Interstitial lamellae = old osteon remnants; between intact osteons.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Accumulation of interstitial lamellae increases with age.

questions.question: Woven bone is characterized by:

options.explanation: That describes lamellar bone.
Woven bone has disorganized collagen fibers and is typical of embryonic bone and fracture callus.
Woven bone contains many osteocytes.
Osteons are in lamellar bone.
It is less mineralized than mature bone.

explanation.overview: Woven bone is an immature, temporary type of bone with haphazard collagen fiber orientation. It is formed rapidly during development and fracture repair and is later replaced by lamellar bone.
explanation.highYield: Woven bone = disorganized collagen, immature; replaced by lamellar bone.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Paget's disease of bone shows mosaic pattern of woven and lamellar bone.

questions.question: The periosteum is attached to bone by:

options.explanation: Sharpey's fibers are bundles of collagen that anchor periosteum to bone.
Not the primary anchoring.
Reticular fibers are in soft organs.
Not present in periosteum.
Tight junctions are cell junctions.

explanation.overview: Sharpey's fibers are thick collagen bundles that penetrate the outer circumferential lamellae of bone, anchoring the periosteum firmly to the bone surface.
explanation.highYield: Sharpey's fibers = collagen fibers anchoring periosteum to bone.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Periosteal elevation during surgery requires severing Sharpey's fibers.

questions.question: Endosteum lines the:

options.explanation: That's periosteum.

options.text: Inner surface of bone (medullary cavity, trabeculae)
options.explanation: Endosteum covers internal bone surfaces and contains osteoprogenitor cells.
Haversian canals have their own lining.
Volkmann's canals are transverse.
Periosteum is outer.

explanation.overview: Endosteum is a thin layer of osteoprogenitor cells and connective tissue lining the medullary cavity and trabeculae. It contributes to bone remodeling and repair.
explanation.highYield: Endosteum = internal lining; source of osteoblasts/osteoclasts for remodeling.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endosteal bone resorption increases with age, expanding the medullary cavity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the extracellular matrix?

options.explanation: Collagen is a major ECM fiber.
Elastin is an ECM protein.
Fibronectin is an ECM glycoprotein.
Actin is a cytoskeletal protein inside cells, not part of the ECM.
Laminin is a basement membrane component.

explanation.overview: The extracellular matrix consists of structural proteins (collagen, elastin), multiadhesive glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin), and proteoglycans. Actin is an intracellular cytoskeletal protein.
explanation.highYield: ECM: collagen, elastin, fibronectin, laminin, proteoglycans. Actin = intracellular.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Anti-actin antibodies are seen in autoimmune hepatitis (smooth muscle antibodies).

questions.question: Fibronectin is an ECM glycoprotein that functions in:

options.explanation: Fibronectin binds integrins and ECM components, mediating cell adhesion and migration.
Calcium deposition is related to bone proteins.
Elasticity is provided by elastin.
Cross-linking is by lysyl oxidase.
Proteoglycan aggregation involves hyaluronic acid and link proteins.

explanation.overview: Fibronectin is a dimeric glycoprotein that binds to integrins and other ECM components like collagen and heparin. It plays a key role in cell adhesion, spreading, and migration during development and wound healing.
explanation.highYield: Fibronectin = cell adhesion (RGD sequence), wound healing, migration.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Plasma fibronectin levels decrease in severe trauma and sepsis.

questions.question: Laminin is a major component of:

options.explanation: Collagen fibrils are mainly collagen.
Laminin is a key glycoprotein in the basal lamina of basement membranes.
Elastic fibers contain elastin and fibrillin.
Reticular fibers are type III collagen.
Ground substance is primarily GAGs and proteoglycans.

explanation.overview: Laminin is a large, cross-shaped glycoprotein found in all basement membranes. It self-assembles into a sheet and interacts with epithelial cells via integrins, anchoring them to the basal lamina.
explanation.highYield: Laminin = basement membrane; epithelial cell anchoring.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in laminin genes cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa.

questions.question: Tenascin is an ECM protein that is prominent during:

options.explanation: Tenascin is expressed during tissue remodeling and development.
Bone mineralization involves osteocalcin, osteopontin.
Elastic fibers involve fibrillin and elastin.
Collagen synthesis is continuous, not specific to tenascin.
Tenascin not primarily adipogenic.

explanation.overview: Tenascin-C is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that is highly expressed during embryogenesis, wound healing, and inflammation. It modulates cell adhesion and migration.
explanation.highYield: Tenascin = embryonic/wound ECM; anti-adhesive properties.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tenascin-C is upregulated in tumors and may promote invasion.

questions.question: Which enzyme is responsible for cross‑linking collagen fibrils?

options.explanation: Collagenase degrades collagen.
Lysyl oxidase deaminates lysine residues, forming cross‑links that stabilize collagen.
Prolyl hydroxylase modifies proline for helix stability, not cross-linking.
Elastase degrades elastin.
Hyaluronidase degrades hyaluronic acid.

explanation.overview: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that oxidatively deaminates lysine and hydroxylysine residues to form aldehydes, which then condense to form covalent cross-links between collagen molecules, providing tensile strength.
explanation.highYield: Lysyl oxidase = copper-dependent; collagen cross-linking; inhibited by β-aminopropionitrile.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Deficiency of lysyl oxidase causes lathyrism, leading to weak connective tissues.

questions.question: Scurvy results from a deficiency in which vitamin, impairing collagen synthesis?

options.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency affects vision and epithelia.
B12 deficiency causes anemia and neurological issues.
Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, essential for stable collagen triple helix.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets/osteomalacia.
Vitamin K is for clotting factors and osteocalcin.

explanation.overview: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a cofactor for prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues in collagen. Without it, collagen is underhydroxylated and weak, leading to scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing).
explanation.highYield: Vitamin C = collagen hydroxylation; deficiency → scurvy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Scurvy presents with perifollicular hemorrhages, gingival swelling, and impaired wound healing.

questions.question: In osteogenesis imperfecta, there is a defect in:

options.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is caused by mutations in type I collagen genes.
Type II collagen mutations cause chondrodysplasias.
Type III mutations cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos.
Type IV mutations cause Alport syndrome.
Elastin defects cause Williams syndrome.

explanation.overview: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a genetic disorder of type I collagen, resulting in brittle bones, blue sclerae, and hearing loss. Most cases are autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2.
explanation.highYield: OI = type I collagen defect; brittle bones.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Severe OI (type II) is lethal in the perinatal period.

questions.question: Ehlers‑Danlos syndrome typically involves defects in:

options.explanation: Ehlers‑Danlos syndromes are a group of disorders affecting collagen, leading to hypermobility and skin fragility.
Elastin defect is Williams syndrome.
Fibrillin defect is Marfan syndrome.
Not primarily.
Laminin defects cause epidermolysis bullosa.

explanation.overview: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) are a heterogeneous group of inherited connective tissue disorders characterized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility. Many subtypes involve defects in collagen synthesis or processing.
explanation.highYield: EDS = collagen defect; hypermobile joints, stretchy skin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vascular EDS (type IV) involves type III collagen defect, causing arterial rupture.

questions.question: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene for:

options.explanation: Collagen I is OI.
Marfan syndrome results from fibrillin‑1 mutations, affecting elastic tissue (cardiovascular, skeletal, ocular).
Elastin defect is Williams syndrome.
Lysyl oxidase defect is lathyrism.
Not Marfan.

explanation.overview: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, a major component of elastic microfibrils. It affects the cardiovascular system, eyes, and skeleton.
explanation.highYield: Marfan = fibrillin-1 mutation; aortic root dilation, lens dislocation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: β-blockers or losartan are used to slow aortic root dilation.

questions.question: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the basement membrane include:

options.explanation: Perlecan is a heparan sulfate proteoglycan in basement membranes.
Aggrecan is in cartilage.
Versican is in loose CT.
Decorin binds collagen fibrils.
Biglycan is a small proteoglycan in bone and other tissues.

explanation.overview: Perlecan is a large heparan sulfate proteoglycan found in all basement membranes, where it contributes to the filtration barrier and binds growth factors.
explanation.highYield: Perlecan = basement membrane proteoglycan; heparan sulfate chains.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Perlecan mutations cause Schwartz-Jampel syndrome (chondrodystrophic myotonia).

questions.question: Decorin is a small proteoglycan that binds to:

options.explanation: Decorin binds collagen fibrils and regulates fibrillogenesis.
Hyaluronic acid binds aggrecan, versican.
Elastin-associated microfibrils have fibrillin.
Decorin primarily decorates collagen.
Laminin is basement membrane.

explanation.overview: Decorin is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) with a dermatan sulfate chain. It binds to the surface of type I collagen fibrils, regulating their diameter and spacing.
explanation.highYield: Decorin = 'decorates' collagen fibrils; regulates fibril assembly.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Decorin has anti-fibrotic properties and is being investigated for scar reduction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a glycosaminoglycan found in large quantities in cartilage?

options.explanation: Chondroitin sulfate is abundant in cartilage proteoglycans like aggrecan.
Dermatan sulfate is in skin, tendons.
Heparan sulfate is in basement membranes, cell surfaces.
Keratan sulfate is present but chondroitin sulfate is more abundant in cartilage.
Hyaluronic acid is unsulfated GAG, also present but not sulfated GAG in proteoglycans.

explanation.overview: Cartilage matrix is rich in proteoglycans like aggrecan, which contain numerous chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains. Chondroitin sulfate provides fixed negative charges that attract water, resisting compression.
explanation.highYield: Cartilage GAGs: chondroitin sulfate (most abundant), keratan sulfate.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Chondroitin sulfate supplements are used for osteoarthritis, though efficacy varies.

questions.question: The most abundant cell type in connective tissue proper is the:

options.explanation: Fibroblasts are the most numerous cells in connective tissue proper.
Macrophages are less numerous than fibroblasts.
Mast cells are relatively scarce.
Adipocytes are abundant in adipose tissue, not general CT proper.
Plasma cells are rare except in inflammation.

explanation.overview: Fibroblasts are the principal cells of connective tissue proper, responsible for synthesizing and maintaining the extracellular matrix. They are spindle-shaped with elongated nuclei.
explanation.highYield: Fibroblast = most common cell in CT proper; synthesizes ECM.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myofibroblasts (activated fibroblasts) play a key role in wound contraction.

questions.question: Kupffer cells are specialized macrophages found in the:

options.explanation: Kupffer cells line the sinusoids of the liver and phagocytose debris.
Alveolar macrophages are in lung.
Spleen has sinus macrophages.
Microglia are in the brain.
Bone marrow has resident macrophages.

explanation.overview: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids. They filter portal blood, removing pathogens, aged erythrocytes, and debris.
explanation.highYield: Kupffer cells = liver macrophages; sinusoidal lining.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Kupffer cell activation contributes to liver inflammation and fibrosis.

questions.question: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the:

options.explanation: Microglia are the immune cells of the CNS, derived from yolk sac progenitors.
Schwann cells and macrophages are in PNS.
Langerhans cells are dendritic cells in skin.
Alveolar macrophages in lung.
Mesangial cells and macrophages in kidney.

explanation.overview: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the CNS. They originate from yolk sac precursors and are self-maintaining. They constantly survey the brain parenchyma and respond to injury.
explanation.highYield: Microglia = CNS macrophages; yolk sac origin; ramified (resting) or activated.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Microglial activation is implicated in neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's).

questions.question: Osteoid refers to:

options.explanation: Mineralized matrix is bone.
Osteoid is newly formed organic bone matrix before mineralization.
Cartilage matrix is different.
Dentine is tooth structure.
Cementum is part of tooth.

explanation.overview: Osteoid is the unmineralized organic portion of bone matrix, composed mainly of type I collagen and non-collagenous proteins. It is secreted by osteoblasts and later mineralizes with hydroxyapatite.
explanation.highYield: Osteoid = unmineralized bone matrix; type I collagen + osteocalcin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteoid accumulation is seen in osteomalacia due to defective mineralization.

questions.question: Which cell type is responsible for bone resorption?

options.explanation: Osteoblasts form bone.
Osteocytes maintain matrix.
Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells that resorb bone by secreting acid and enzymes.
Osteoprogenitors differentiate into osteoblasts.
Chondroclasts resorb cartilage, but not bone.

explanation.overview: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells of hematopoietic origin that adhere to bone and create a sealed acidic environment (Howship's lacuna) to dissolve mineral and degrade collagen.
explanation.highYield: Osteoclast = bone resorption; acid + cathepsin K.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bisphosphonates induce osteoclast apoptosis, reducing bone loss in osteoporosis.

questions.question: The zone of provisional calcification in endochondral ossification occurs in the:

options.explanation: In the epiphyseal plate, the zone of provisional calcification is where cartilage matrix mineralizes.
Periosteum is the outer covering.
Diaphysis is the shaft.
Metaphysis is the region adjacent to growth plate.
Articular cartilage persists, not calcifies in growth.

explanation.overview: The zone of provisional calcification is a layer in the epiphyseal plate where cartilage matrix becomes calcified and chondrocytes die, providing a scaffold for bone deposition.
explanation.highYield: Zone of provisional calcification = calcified cartilage in growth plate.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In rickets, this zone is wide and uncalcified due to vitamin D deficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a syndesmosis?

options.explanation: Sutures are a different type of fibrous joint with very little movement.
A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint with more distance between bones, e.g., interosseous membrane.
Gomphosis is the tooth socket joint.
Synchondrosis is a cartilaginous joint.
Symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint.

explanation.overview: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint where bones are connected by a ligament or an interosseous membrane, allowing limited movement. Examples include the distal tibiofibular joint and the interosseous membrane of the forearm.
explanation.highYield: Syndesmosis = fibrous joint, more distance between bones; interosseous membrane.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: High ankle sprain involves injury to the tibiofibular syndesmosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of fibrous joint?

options.explanation: Suture is a fibrous joint (skull).
Gomphosis is a fibrous joint (tooth).
Syndesmosis is fibrous.
Synchondrosis is a cartilaginous joint (primary cartilaginous), not fibrous.
Synchondrosis is the correct answer.

explanation.overview: Fibrous joints (synarthroses) are connected by dense connective tissue. They include sutures, gomphoses, and syndesmoses. Synchondroses are cartilaginous joints connected by hyaline cartilage.
explanation.highYield: Fibrous joints: suture, gomphosis, syndesmosis. Synchondrosis = cartilaginous.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of sutures.

questions.question: The articular cartilage of synovial joints is:

options.explanation: Fibrocartilage is in discs and menisci.
Articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage.
Elastic cartilage is in ear, epiglottis.
Not a standard type.
Calcified cartilage is a zone in the growth plate.

explanation.overview: Articular cartilage covering the ends of bones in synovial joints is hyaline cartilage. It is avascular and lacks perichondrium, receiving nutrients from synovial fluid.
explanation.highYield: Articular cartilage = hyaline; no perichondrium; lubricated by synovial fluid.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteoarthritis involves progressive loss of articular cartilage.

questions.question: Which ligament contains the ligamentum flavum, rich in elastin?

options.explanation: ACL is dense regular.
Ligamentum nuchae is also elastic but not flavum.
Ligamentum flavum connects vertebral laminae and contains high proportion of elastic fibers.
Patellar ligament is dense regular.
MCL is dense regular.

explanation.overview: The ligamentum flavum is an elastic ligament connecting the laminae of adjacent vertebrae, helping maintain posture and assisting with spinal extension.
explanation.highYield: Ligamentum flavum = elastic tissue; yellow color; spinal laminae.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hypertrophy of ligamentum flavum can contribute to spinal stenosis.

questions.question: The annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc is composed of:

options.explanation: Hyaline cartilage is not the main component.
The annulus fibrosus is fibrocartilage with concentric lamellae of collagen.
Not elastic.
It is fibrocartilage, not pure dense regular.
Annulus is organized lamellae.

explanation.overview: The annulus fibrosus is the outer part of the intervertebral disc, made of concentric layers of fibrocartilage. It contains type I collagen fibers oriented obliquely in alternating directions to withstand torsional stress.
explanation.highYield: Annulus fibrosus = fibrocartilage; concentric lamellae of type I collagen.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tears in the annulus fibrosus can lead to disc herniation.

questions.question: The nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc is derived from:

options.explanation: Annulus fibrosus from mesenchyme, not nucleus pulposus.
The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the embryonic notochord.
Somites give rise to vertebrae and muscles.
Neural crest forms PNS, melanocytes.
Ectoderm forms skin and neural tube.

explanation.overview: The nucleus pulposus is the gel-like center of the intervertebral disc, derived from the notochord. It contains high water and proteoglycan content, providing shock absorption.
explanation.highYield: Nucleus pulposus = notochord remnant; high water, aggrecan.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Desiccation of the nucleus pulposus with age contributes to disc degeneration.

questions.question: Which vitamin is essential for the synthesis of γ‑carboxyglutamate in clotting factors and bone proteins?

options.explanation: Vitamin A for vision and epithelia.
B12 for DNA synthesis.
Vitamin C for collagen hydroxylation.
Vitamin D for calcium absorption.
Vitamin K is a cofactor for γ‑glutamyl carboxylase, modifying proteins like osteocalcin.

explanation.overview: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin required for the carboxylation of glutamic acid residues to γ-carboxyglutamate in proteins such as clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and osteocalcin, enabling calcium binding.
explanation.highYield: Vitamin K = γ-carboxylation; clotting factors and osteocalcin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, acting as an anticoagulant.

questions.question: Osteocalcin is a protein secreted by osteoblasts that:

options.explanation: Mineralization is initiated by matrix vesicles.
Osteocalcin binds calcium but also has other roles.
Osteocalcin may influence, but it's not the primary regulator.
Osteocalcin is involved in bone mineralization and calcium homeostasis.
It does have functions.

explanation.overview: Osteocalcin (bone Gla protein) is a vitamin K-dependent, calcium-binding protein produced by osteoblasts. It regulates mineralization and may act as a hormone influencing energy metabolism and testosterone production.
explanation.highYield: Osteocalcin = bone-specific; vitamin K-dependent; calcium binding; marker of bone formation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Serum osteocalcin levels are used to assess bone turnover in osteoporosis.

questions.question: In rheumatoid arthritis, the synovial membrane shows:

options.text: Hypertrophy and villous formation with inflammatory infiltrate
options.explanation: Rheumatoid synovitis features hyperplasia, villi, and chronic inflammation.
That's more like osteoarthritis.
It is inflamed.
Calcification is not typical.
Not a feature.

explanation.overview: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease causing synovial membrane inflammation (synovitis), hyperplasia, villous hypertrophy, and infiltration by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, leading to pannus formation and joint destruction.
explanation.highYield: RA synovium = hyperplasia, villi, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of osteomalacia?

options.explanation: Excessive mineralization is osteopetrosis.
Osteomalacia (rickets in children) results from defective mineralization of osteoid, often due to vitamin D deficiency.
Bone density is decreased.
Structure is abnormal.
Osteoclast activity may be normal or increased, but not the primary defect.

explanation.overview: Osteomalacia is softening of bones due to defective mineralization of osteoid, typically from vitamin D deficiency or abnormal vitamin D metabolism. It leads to bone pain, fractures, and muscle weakness.
explanation.highYield: Osteomalacia = poor mineralization; wide osteoid seams; low calcium/phosphate.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Renal osteodystrophy can cause osteomalacia due to impaired vitamin D activation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most abundant type of collagen in the human body?

options.explanation: Type II is mainly in cartilage.
Type I collagen comprises about 90% of body collagen, found in bone, skin, tendons.
Type III is reticular fibers.
Type IV is basement membrane.
Type X is in hypertrophic cartilage.

explanation.overview: Type I collagen is the most prevalent collagen in the body, forming the main structural protein in bone, skin, tendons, and ligaments.
explanation.highYield: Type I collagen = most abundant; bone, skin, tendons, ligaments.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Osteogenesis imperfecta is due to type I collagen mutations.

questions.question: The main difference between white and brown adipose tissue is:

options.text: White fat has a single lipid droplet; brown fat has multiple droplets and more mitochondria
options.explanation: White adipocytes are unilocular; brown adipocytes are multilocular with abundant mitochondria for thermogenesis.
Brown fat has more mitochondria.

options.text: White fat is only found in children
options.explanation: White fat is throughout life.
Brown fat is highly vascularized.
They are distinct.

explanation.overview: White adipose tissue stores energy as a single large lipid droplet, while brown adipose tissue dissipates energy as heat, with multiple small lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria containing UCP1.
explanation.highYield: White fat = unilocular, energy storage; Brown fat = multilocular, heat production.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Brown fat activation is a potential target for weight loss.

questions.question: Hyaluronidase is an enzyme that breaks down:

options.explanation: Collagenase breaks down collagen.
Hyaluronidase degrades hyaluronic acid, reducing viscosity of ground substance.
Elastase breaks elastin.
Proteases degrade proteoglycans.
Specific proteases degrade fibronectin.

explanation.overview: Hyaluronidase cleaves hyaluronic acid, decreasing the viscosity of the extracellular matrix. It is produced by sperm to penetrate the cumulus oophorus, and by some bacteria to invade tissues.
explanation.highYield: Hyaluronidase = breaks hyaluronic acid; bacterial spread factor, sperm penetration.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hyaluronidase is used clinically to enhance drug dispersion.

questions.question: Which type of collagen is found exclusively in the basement membrane?

options.explanation: Type I is fibrillar, in bone, skin.
Type II is in cartilage.
Type III is reticular.
Type IV collagen forms a meshwork in basement membranes.
Type V is a minor fibrillar collagen.

explanation.overview: Type IV collagen is a non-fibrillar, network-forming collagen that is the primary structural component of the basement membrane, interacting with laminin and proteoglycans.
explanation.highYield: Type IV collagen = basement membrane; network-forming; not fibrillar.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in type IV collagen cause Alport syndrome (kidney, ear, eye).

questions.question: The most common cell type found in the dermis is the:

options.explanation: Macrophages are present but not most numerous.
Fibroblasts are the primary cells of the dermis, producing collagen and elastin.
Mast cells are scattered.
Melanocytes are in the epidermis.
Langerhans cells are in the epidermis.

explanation.overview: The dermis is a connective tissue layer rich in fibroblasts, which synthesize and maintain the collagenous and elastic extracellular matrix that provides skin strength and elasticity.
explanation.highYield: Dermis main cell = fibroblast; produces collagen, elastin, ground substance.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dermal fibroblasts are key in wound healing and scar formation.

questions.question: Which staining method is used to demonstrate reticular fibers?

options.explanation: H&E stains collagen pink; reticular fibers are difficult to differentiate.
Reticular fibers are argyrophilic and stain black with silver stains.
Masson's stains collagen blue/green but not specific for reticular.
Verhoeff's stains elastic fibers.
Alcian blue stains acidic GAGs.

explanation.overview: Reticular fibers (type III collagen) are thin and PAS-positive. They are best visualized with silver impregnation techniques (e.g., Gomori's), where they appear black against a lighter background.
explanation.highYield: Reticular fibers = silver stain (argyrophilic); black.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Silver staining is used to assess liver fibrosis (reticulin framework).

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of integrins?

options.explanation: Tight junctions are formed by claudins and occludins.
Integrins are transmembrane receptors that bind ECM components (e.g., fibronectin, collagen) and transduce signals.
That's ion channels.
Collagen synthesis is by fibroblasts.
That's by specific enzymes.

explanation.overview: Integrins are αβ heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that link the extracellular matrix to the actin cytoskeleton, mediating adhesion, migration, and bidirectional signaling (outside-in, inside-out).
explanation.highYield: Integrins = cell-ECM adhesion; bind RGD motif; signaling.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Integrin antagonists are used as antiplatelet drugs (e.g., abciximab).

questions.question: The ground substance in Wharton's jelly is particularly rich in:

options.explanation: Collagen is sparse.
Wharton's jelly has a high concentration of hyaluronic acid, giving it a gelatinous consistency.
Elastin is not abundant.
Keratan sulfate is in cartilage and cornea.
Laminin is in basement membrane.

explanation.overview: Wharton's jelly is mucous connective tissue with abundant hyaluronic acid, which binds water and creates a thick, protective gel around umbilical vessels.
explanation.highYield: Wharton's jelly = hyaluronic acid-rich; hydrated gel.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Stem cells harvested from Wharton's jelly are used in regenerative medicine.

questions.question: Keloid scars are characterized by:

options.explanation: That is a different scar type.

options.text: Excessive deposition of collagen beyond wound margins
options.explanation: Keloids result from overactive fibroblasts, producing thick, raised collagen that extends beyond the original injury.
There is excessive collagen.
Not the primary feature.
Scar tissue is not normal regeneration.

explanation.overview: Keloids are benign fibrous proliferations in which excessive type I and III collagen is deposited, growing beyond the boundaries of the original wound. They are more common in dark-skinned individuals.
explanation.highYield: Keloid = excessive collagen, extends beyond wound margins.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment includes intralesional steroids, pressure therapy, and surgery.

questions.question: The tooth socket (gomphosis) is an example of which type of joint?

options.explanation: A gomphosis is a fibrous joint where the tooth is anchored by the periodontal ligament.
That would be synchondrosis or symphysis.
Synovial joints have a cavity.
Amphiarthrosis is a slightly movable joint, often cartilaginous.
Diarthrosis is freely movable, like synovial.

explanation.overview: A gomphosis is a specialized fibrous joint in which a conical peg (tooth root) fits into a socket (alveolus) and is held by the periodontal ligament.
explanation.highYield: Gomphosis = fibrous joint; tooth in socket; periodontal ligament.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Periodontitis damages the periodontal ligament, loosening the tooth.

questions.question: Which type of connective tissue forms the lamina propria of mucous membranes?

options.explanation: Lamina propria is loose, not dense.
The lamina propria is a layer of loose connective tissue beneath the epithelium of mucous membranes.
Tendons/ligaments.
Reticular is in lymphoid organs.
Elastic tissue in large arteries.

explanation.overview: The lamina propria is a loose connective tissue layer that underlies the epithelia of mucous membranes, providing vascular, immune, and structural support.
explanation.highYield: Lamina propria = loose (areolar) CT; under epithelium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Inflammatory cells infiltrate the lamina propria in many mucosal infections.

questions.question: Mast cells can be distinguished histologically by their:

options.explanation: Mast cell granules are basophilic, not eosinophilic.
Mast cells contain numerous basophilic granules that stain metachromatically with toluidine blue.
Mast cells are mononuclear; osteoclasts are multinucleated.
Plasma cells have abundant rough ER.
Fibroblasts are spindle-shaped.

explanation.overview: Mast cells are oval or round cells with a central nucleus and abundant basophilic secretory granules containing heparin and histamine. They stain metachromatically with toluidine blue.
explanation.highYield: Mast cell = basophilic granules, metachromatic; IgE receptors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mastocytosis is a clonal proliferation of mast cells.

questions.question: Which of the following is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) that regulates collagen fibrillogenesis?

options.explanation: Aggrecan is a large aggregating proteoglycan of cartilage.
Decorin is a SLRP that binds to type I collagen fibrils and controls their diameter.
Perlecan is a heparan sulfate proteoglycan of basement membrane.
Versican is a large proteoglycan, not SLRP.
Syndecan is a cell-surface proteoglycan.

explanation.overview: Decorin is a prototype small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) that 'decorates' the surface of collagen fibrils, limiting their lateral growth and affecting tissue mechanics.
explanation.highYield: Decorin = SLRP; decorates collagen I; regulates fibril size.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Decorin deficiency leads to fragile skin and abnormal collagen fibrils.

questions.question: The main type of collagen in the vitreous humor of the eye is:

options.explanation: Type I is in sclera and cornea mainly.
The vitreous humor contains type II collagen, forming a gel-like matrix.
Type III is reticular.
Type IV is basement membrane.
Type V is minor fibrillar.

explanation.overview: The vitreous body is a transparent gel composed of type II collagen fibrils and hyaluronic acid, providing structural support to the eye.
explanation.highYield: Vitreous = type II collagen + hyaluronic acid; gel-like.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vitreous liquefaction occurs with aging and in high myopia.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a cartilaginous joint that ossifies with age?

options.explanation: Symphysis does not typically ossify.
Sutures are fibrous joints that can fuse.
Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) often ossify, e.g., epiphyseal plates.
Synovial joint.
Fibrous joint.

explanation.overview: Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints where hyaline cartilage directly connects bones. They are temporary and often ossify, converting to synostoses, as in the epiphyseal plate and first sternocostal joint.
explanation.highYield: Synchondrosis = hyaline cartilage joint; ossifies with age (e.g., growth plate).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fusion of synchondroses is used to estimate skeletal age.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of connective tissue?

options.explanation: That is one function.
Adipose tissue stores energy.
Connective tissue houses immune cells.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue.
Connective tissue performs all these functions.

explanation.overview: Connective tissues serve diverse roles: structural support (bone, cartilage), binding (tendons, ligaments), energy storage (adipose), immune surveillance (lymphoid tissue), and transport (blood).
explanation.highYield: Connective tissue functions: support, protection, storage, transport, defense.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dysfunction of connective tissue underlies many systemic diseases.

questions.question: The extracellular matrix of bone is unique because it contains:

options.explanation: Type II is in cartilage.
Bone matrix is mineralized with hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2].
Bone has minimal elastin.
Ground substance is solid due to mineralization.
Bone has type I collagen, not III.

explanation.overview: Bone ECM is specialized by the deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals within and around type I collagen fibrils, providing both compressive and tensile strength.
explanation.highYield: Bone matrix = type I collagen + hydroxyapatite (mineral).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Demineralization of bone occurs in osteoporosis and rickets.

questions.question: A young patient presents with hypermobile joints, hyperelastic skin, and easy bruising. Which connective tissue component is most likely defective?

options.explanation: Fibrillin defect is Marfan syndrome.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves collagen defects, leading to hypermobility and skin fragility.
Elastin defect is Williams syndrome.
Laminin defects cause skin blistering.
Not the typical EDS.

explanation.overview: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is caused by defects in collagen synthesis or structure, presenting with joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.
explanation.highYield: EDS = collagen defect; hypermobile joints, stretchy skin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vascular EDS (COL3A1 mutation) can cause arterial rupture.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key component of the basement membrane that binds to both cells and ECM?

options.explanation: Elastin is not in basement membrane.
Laminin is a large glycoprotein in the basal lamina that binds to integrins, type IV collagen, and perlecan.
Fibrillin is in elastic microfibrils.
Hyaluronic acid is in ground substance, not basement membrane.
Decorin is associated with collagen fibrils.

explanation.overview: Laminin is a cruciform glycoprotein unique to basement membranes. It self-assembles into a network and binds to epithelial cells via integrins and dystroglycan, and to type IV collagen and perlecan, forming a structural bridge.
explanation.highYield: Laminin = basement membrane 'glue'; binds cells to ECM.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Autoantibodies to laminin cause mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.question: Cartilage is considered a specialized connective tissue because it:

options.explanation: Cartilage is avascular.

options.text: Has a firm extracellular matrix that resists compression
options.explanation: Cartilage has a specialized ECM rich in proteoglycans and type II collagen, providing resilience.
Cartilage cells are chondrocytes.
Only elastic cartilage has abundant elastin.
Cartilage is mesodermal.

explanation.overview: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue with a firm, gel-like matrix that provides support and resists compression. It is avascular and consists of chondrocytes embedded in a matrix rich in type II collagen and aggrecan.
explanation.highYield: Cartilage = firm ECM, type II collagen, aggrecan; avascular.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Damage to cartilage is difficult to repair because of its avascular nature.

questions.question: The cells that maintain the extracellular matrix of connective tissue are called:

options.explanation: Fibroblasts actively synthesize ECM; fibrocytes are their quiescent counterparts that maintain the matrix.
Mast cells release granules, not ECM maintenance.
Plasma cells produce antibodies.
Macrophages are phagocytic.
Adipocytes store fat.

explanation.overview: Fibroblasts are the active cells that produce and secrete ECM components. In mature, less active tissue, they become fibrocytes, which maintain the matrix.
explanation.highYield: Fibroblast (active) / fibrocyte (quiescent) = maintain ECM.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fibroblast senescence contributes to impaired wound healing in the elderly.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about tendons?

options.text: They have high proteoglycan content and resist compression
options.explanation: That's cartilage.

options.text: They are composed of dense regular connective tissue with parallel collagen bundles
options.explanation: Tendons consist of dense regular CT with collagen fibers aligned in the direction of pull.
Tendons have poor blood supply.
Tendons have minimal elastin.
They are poorly vascularized, not completely avascular.

explanation.overview: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue with tightly packed, parallel type I collagen fibers and few elongated fibroblasts (tenocytes), optimized for transmitting muscle force to bone.
explanation.highYield: Tendon = dense regular CT; parallel collagen; resists tension.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tendon injuries (tendinopathy) are common in overuse and heal slowly.

questions.question: Which molecule acts as a linker between aggrecan and hyaluronic acid in cartilage?

options.explanation: Decorin binds collagen.
Link protein stabilizes the binding of aggrecan monomers to hyaluronic acid, forming large proteoglycan aggregates.
Fibronectin binds integrins and ECM.
Laminin is in basement membrane.
Tenascin modulates adhesion.

explanation.overview: In cartilage, aggrecan monomers non-covalently bind to a hyaluronic acid filament, and this interaction is stabilized by a small protein called link protein, forming massive proteoglycan aggregates that provide compressive resistance.
explanation.highYield: Aggrecan + hyaluronic acid + link protein = cartilage aggregate.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Degradation of link protein and aggrecan by aggrecanases occurs early in osteoarthritis.

questions.question: The periodontal ligament is classified as:

options.explanation: It's more specialized.
Not exactly.

options.text: A specialized fibrous joint (gomphosis) with dense regular CT
options.explanation: The periodontal ligament is dense regular connective tissue that forms a gomphosis, anchoring the tooth.
It is dense.
Not elastic.

explanation.overview: The periodontal ligament is a specialized dense regular connective tissue that connects cementum of the tooth root to alveolar bone, forming a gomphosis joint. It contains collagen fibers (Sharpey's fibers) inserted into bone and cementum.
explanation.highYield: Periodontal ligament = dense regular CT; gomphosis; Sharpey's fibers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Periodontitis leads to destruction of the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone loss.

questions.question: Which embryonic tissue gives rise to the axial skeleton and dermis?

options.explanation: Endoderm forms gut and respiratory epithelium.
Ectoderm forms epidermis and nervous system.
Somites from paraxial mesoderm give rise to axial skeleton, muscles, and dermis.
Neural crest forms facial bones and PNS.
Notochord induces neural tube but does not directly form axial skeleton.

explanation.overview: The paraxial mesoderm condenses into somites, which differentiate into sclerotome (axial skeleton), dermatome (dermis), and myotome (skeletal muscle).
explanation.highYield: Somites → sclerotome (bone), dermatome (dermis), myotome (muscle).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of somitogenesis can cause vertebral anomalies (e.g., spondylocostal dysostosis).

questions.question: The enzyme responsible for removing collagen fibrils during tissue remodeling is:

options.explanation: Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen.
MMPs, like collagenase (MMP-1), cleave collagen at specific sites, initiating degradation.
Prolyl hydroxylase is for collagen synthesis.
Hyaluronidase degrades hyaluronic acid.
Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide.

explanation.overview: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that degrade ECM components. Collagenases (MMP-1, -8, -13) specifically cleave fibrillar collagens, enabling tissue remodeling.
explanation.highYield: MMPs (collagenases) degrade collagen; important in remodeling, wound healing.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) balance MMP activity; imbalance leads to pathological tissue destruction.

questions.question: In scurvy, impaired collagen synthesis leads to which of the following symptoms?

options.explanation: That's more rickets/OI.

options.text: Gum bleeding, poor wound healing, and petechiae
options.explanation: Defective collagen in blood vessel walls and oral mucosa leads to bleeding and impaired healing.
That's EDS.
That's Marfan.
Not typical of scurvy.

explanation.overview: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen hydroxylation, leading to fragile capillaries, easy bruising, swollen bleeding gums, and poor wound healing—hallmarks of scurvy.
explanation.highYield: Scurvy: bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, impaired wound healing.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Scurvy is rare now but seen in malnutrition and alcoholics.

questions.question: Tropoelastin is secreted by fibroblasts and assembles into elastic fibers by:

options.explanation: Elastin cross-links with other elastin molecules via desmosine.

options.text: Associating with fibrillin microfibrils and cross-linking via lysyl oxidase
options.explanation: Tropoelastin is deposited onto a scaffold of fibrillin microfibrils and cross-linked by lysyl oxidase to form mature elastin.
Not the main assembly.
Triple helix is collagen.
It requires fibrillin.

explanation.overview: Elastic fiber assembly involves the deposition of tropoelastin monomers onto a preformed scaffold of fibrillin-1 microfibrils. Lysyl oxidase then cross-links the tropoelastin to form a functional elastic network.
explanation.highYield: Elastin assembly: fibrillin scaffold + tropoelastin + lysyl oxidase cross-linking.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Defects in fibrillin-1 (Marfan) disrupt elastic fiber assembly.

questions.question: The menisci of the knee are composed of:

The menisci are fibrocartilaginous structures that absorb shock and improve joint congruity.
Elastic cartilage is in ear.

explanation.overview: The menisci (medial and lateral) of the knee are crescent-shaped fibrocartilage pads that distribute load, absorb shock, and stabilize the joint.
explanation.highYield: Meniscus = fibrocartilage; type I collagen; shock absorber.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Meniscal tears are common sports injuries; the outer third has some blood supply for healing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of osteogenesis imperfecta type II?

options.explanation: That's type I.

options.text: Lethal perinatal form with multiple fractures at birth
options.explanation: Type II OI is the most severe, often lethal due to severe skeletal deformities and rib fractures.
Common in type I.
Dental problems occur but not only.
OI often causes short stature.

explanation.overview: Osteogenesis imperfecta type II is the most severe form, resulting from severe type I collagen defects. It is characterized by extreme bone fragility, multiple intrauterine or perinatal fractures, and is often fatal shortly after birth.
explanation.highYield: OI type II = lethal perinatal; severe collagen I defect.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Prenatal ultrasound may detect fractures and shortened long bones.
